core: The working definition of accrual accounting: recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash movement, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (Section 4.1) and corroborated by CFI's Accrual Accounting guide
The revenue recognition principle: revenue is recorded in the period it is earned, not the period it is paid (OpenStax Section 3.1), with an original example (Harborview Painting)
The matching principle (expense recognition principle): expenses are matched with the revenues they helped produce in the period those revenues are earned (OpenStax Section 3.1)
Accrual versus cash: when things count versus when money moves (cash basis records only when cash is exchanged; OpenStax Section 4.1); cash-accounting is a sibling topic, referenced only

Why accrual is the standard: GAAP/IFRS financial statements use accrual accounting because it better matches revenues and expenses and standardizes reporting for comparability (OpenStax Section 4.1); CFI: a more accurate picture of true financial position
The honest framing: accrual accounting is more accurate and more complicated — the trade-off stated plainly (cash basis 'can be simpler to track', OpenStax Section 4.1)
supporting: The time period assumption: results are reported over months, quarters, or years (OpenStax Section 3.1)
GAAP as the accounting standards, conventions, and rules companies use to measure financial results (SEC Investor.gov glossary)
Neither GAAP nor IFRS allows cash accounting (CFI)
Accrued revenues and accrued expenses as the two broad categories of accruals (CFI)
outOfScope: Cash-basis accounting mechanics (sibling topic accounting:foundations:cash-accounting; referenced only)
Adjusting entries and period-end adjustments (sibling topic accounting:foundations:adjusting-entries; referenced only)
Revenue accounts and revenue recognition detail (sibling topic accounting:foundations:revenue; referenced only)
Expense types and expense accounts (sibling topic accounting:foundations:expenses; referenced only)
The income statement's structure and preparation (sibling topic accounting:foundations:income-statement; referenced only)
U.S. tax rules on cash versus accrual methods (noted as a nuance in conflictingEvidence, not taught)

claims.claim: Accrual basis accounting prescribes that revenues and expenses are recorded in the accounting period in which they were earned or incurred, no matter when cash receipts or payments occur; in this lesson accrual accounting is defined as recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash movement.

The revenue recognition principle directs a company to recognize revenue in the period in which it is earned — revenue is not considered earned until a product or service has been provided — and there does not have to be a correlation between when cash is collected and when revenue is recognized.

The expense recognition principle, also known as the matching principle, requires expenses to be matched with associated revenues in the period in which the revenues were earned; recording expenses separately from the revenues they generated makes statements unreliable.

Cash basis accounting records transactions in the financial statements only when there is an exchange of cash; it can delay or accelerate revenue and expense reporting until cash receipts or outlays occur, and it can be simpler to track than accrual basis accounting.
Companies, public or private, using US GAAP or IFRS prepare their financial statements using the rules of accrual accounting; CFI states that neither GAAP nor IFRS allows cash accounting.

The accrual method is considered to better match revenues and expenses and standardizes reporting information for comparability, which matters to external users making investment or lending decisions and to internal users making decisions about performance, budgeting, and growth.

Accrual accounting provides a more accurate picture of a company's true financial position; cash accounting can offer a misleading picture of an entity's financial health when unpaid expenses or outstanding receivables are not represented in the financial statements.

GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) are the accounting standards, conventions, and rules that companies use to measure their financial results, including net income (SEC Investor.gov glossary).

conflictingEvidence: No direct conflicts between the sources. Two nuances are recorded for the record: (1) OpenStax Section 4.1 notes that some nonpublic companies may choose cash basis accounting for reporting, and CFI notes that U.S. tax rules permit cash accounting for sole proprietorships and small businesses — the lesson keeps tax treatment out of scope and states the GAAP financial-reporting rule; (2) the judgment that accrual is 'more accurate' is supported by both OpenStax (better matching, comparability) and CFI (more accurate picture of true financial position), and the lesson balances it with the honest framing that accrual is also more complicated (cash basis 'can be simpler to track').
